title: The Queen of Sheba
hookLine: Bilqis consults her council, tests Sulayman, and submits with him to the Lord of the worlds (27:29–44)

lines: A LETTER IN THE THRONE ROOM.
cards: A letter lands in a throne room in Sheba. Sulayman has sent the hoopoe with it, told to throw it down to them. The queen opens it before her nobles.

It's from a foreign king, and it's short: it opens in the name of God, the Merciful, and tells her not to rise up in pride against him but to come to him in surrender. A letter like that could start a war by evening.
Watch what this queen does instead.

teach.h: A NOBLE LETTER: IN THE NAME OF GOD.
teach.b: First, she reads it to her council, calls it a noble letter, and quotes its opening. Pickthall: "Lo! it is from Solomon, and lo! it is: In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful".
That's the bismillah, inside a surah's verse, in a queen's mouth.

Then she consults: I decide nothing, she tells her chiefs, until you are present. They answer like soldiers: we have strength and great might, but the command is yours. She doesn't reach for the might.
Kings, she says, when they enter a town, ruin it and humble its honored people. So she tests him instead, with a gift, and waits to see what comes back.
Sulayman refuses it: what God has given me is better than what He has given you. Then she travels to him.

teach.h: A GIFT, A THRONE, A FLOOR OF GLASS.
teach.b: Her throne has been brought there before her, disguised, and she's asked: is your throne like this? Her careful answer: it's as though it were the very one.
Then she's led into a hall and, thinking the floor is a pool of water, she lifts her skirt. It's smooth glass. And she speaks the surah's climax.

teach.h: WITH SOLOMON, TO THE LORD OF THE WORLDS.
teach.b: Pickthall: "I surrender with Solomon unto Allah, the Lord of the Worlds." With Solomon, not to him. The Qur'an never gives her name.
Muslim tradition calls her Bilqis; the Hebrew Bible also tells of a Queen of Sheba who visited Solomon with hard questions. In An-Naml, what stands out is her method.
She consulted, avoided war, tested, looked closely, and when she saw, she said so.

how: Muslims often cite the Queen of Sheba's council as an example of shura, consultation, and many pray istikhara, the prayer for guidance, before a big decision.

games.q: you're the queen. a powerful king has written telling you to come in surrender. your chiefs say they're strong and ready. what do you do?
o: send a gift, and watch how he answers.
games.why: she says kings ruin the towns they enter, and tests Sulayman with a gift. he refuses it, and she comes to see for herself.

practice: Bring to mind one decision coming up, a move, a job, a hard conversation, and notice whether you've already decided it alone, quickly.

Think of two or three people whose judgment you trust, and how you'd lay it out for them plainly, the way the queen did. If you pray, you can make istikhara, the prayer for guidance, or simply ask for a clear head.

wordCard.voice: Bilqis. Muslim tradition's name for the Queen of Sheba in An-Naml, who consulted her council, tested Sulayman, looked closely, and surrendered with him to the Lord of the worlds. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Saba', Sheba, the kingdom of the queen; it also names surah thirty-four.

carryVoice: Your line: she thought it through. Her strength was in the asking, not the army. Until tomorrow.
